PRIMARY.pick: DD2 lifecycle-intel, SaaS-only (C-80 price/allocation alerts + C-29 NVM-EOL finder + C-61 LTB sizer and studies), run as a capped, gated side business. It is the best available option, not a venture: no venture-grade PRIMARY exists in this study. If K0, K6 or K1 fails, the PRIMARY becomes NONE (keep the day job and the $40k).
PRIMARY.rationale: Highest expected value for this founder, but only because the test is cheap and the downside is capped. (1) Revised economics (04_DEEPDIVES/lifecycle-intel.md §14.3; models/lifecycle-intel.py re-run 2026-11-01, exit 0). First revenue m6 (2027-05). ARR $69,915 at m18 and $149,629 at m36 in BASE, $104,077 in GLUT and $83,031 in SEVERE. Breakeven with the founder unpaid at m17. The $10k/month salary is never covered in any scenario. Cash low $6,100 at m16, a $33.9k draw on $40k. A 30% miss on price or conversion takes cash to -$11.1k or -$4.9k. (2) Why it beats the field. It has the cheapest decisive test in the record: ~$2,950, 29 days, ~55 h, with nothing built before K0 (§10). It is pure software at 57% GM by m36. Its EOL/lifecycle module holds flat at $5,774/month through the glut (§12). Every other deep dive has negative or roughly zero EV per the phase5 ev_notes: DD1 -$3.5k cumulative EBITDA, DD3 -$29.8k, DD4 -$95.7k cash at m36, DD6 -$29.4k plus a $25k bridge, DD7 ~0. DD5 is weaker; see FALLBACK. (3) My EV [ESTIMATE]. P(K0) ~0.6 x P(K6) ~0.45 x P(K1) ~0.35 gives ~0.09 to pass. In passing worlds, 36-month cash moves +$36.4k BASE, +$6.8k GLUT and -$8.9k SEVERE, plus a small sellable SaaS. Failing worlds lose $0.5-3k. That gives E[cash] of about +$1-3k, and about -$3k net of ~200 expected hours at $25/h. That is indistinguishable from keeping the day job, except that it buys information with a capped loss. (4) Mission integrity, said plainly. It makes no memory and has no U.S.-manufacturing content. It uses none of the three 'cheaper materials' senses. Its Rule-4 axis is supply security and lifecycle foresight for U.S. SMB hardware OEMs. Rule 6: the price module falls 57% in GLUT and 83% in SEVERE, so only the lifecycle line is cycle-proof. Its #3-#5 Phase 3 ranks come from the rubric's cheap/fast/founder-fit bias (03_SCORING.md §6), so do not cite the rank as evidence of quality. The C-86 index is NOT part of this pick: the red team killed it as designed, and it survives only as a separate $0 option (see MOONSHOT). (5) It becomes a venture-grade PRIMARY only if observed trial-to-paid conversion reaches >=14.7%, the model's threshold for covering the salary by m36 (§14.3). Even then it never does so in GLUT.
PRIMARY.gate: K0 by 2026-11-09: a written employer carve-out covering the product, the SMB hardware-OEM industry and third-party PO-price contributions. The day job sits in the buyer persona's industry, so this gate decides everything. If it is refused, stop; build nothing. K6 by ~2026-11-30: 25 qualified calls booked within 21 days from cold outreach outside the employer's network. K1 by 2026-12-01: >=5 of 25 give a refundable $500 deposit or a paid LOI at >=$200/month. Integrity tightening: at least 3 of the 5 must be cash, because the red team's own standard is cash, not LOIs (05_REDTEAM.md, DD6 VC verdict). Failing K6 or K1 kills DD2. K5 by 2026-12-15: Nexar or DigiKey allows in-app prices in writing at <=$1,000/month. If not, re-run K1 on a demo built on public prints; if that fails, kill. After a pass, use the stop rules in §11: >=2 paying accounts by 2027-08-31 (m9); >=5 accounts or MRR >=$1,700 by 2027-11-30 (m12); stop if cash falls below $5k; <13 accounts at m18 means opening exit talks (Lytica, Z2Data, Accuris, Supplyframe, Luminovo); ARR <$78k at m24 means selling or winding down.
PRIMARY.spend: Week of 2026-11-02: <=$500 for one flat-fee employment-agreement review. Have it cover DD5 too, so the fallback needs no second review. Only after K0 is signed: <=$1,450 through 2026-12-01 (Sales Navigator ~$100, 25 x $50 call thank-yous, domain/hosting ~$100). Defer the $1,000 government-contracts consult and the model's $5,000 m2 antitrust opinion until K3 and K4 pass, because both protect only the index; deferring them lifts the BASE cash low from $6.1k to ~$11k [ESTIMATE]. Hard cap on the test: $5,000. After a pass: <=~$22k cumulative through the m9 gate (model cash $18.4k at 2027-08), <=$34k ever (model max draw $33.9k), and never below a $5k cash floor.

FALLBACK.pick: DD5 open-memory-ip, C-33 OpenRAM macro service wedge only (sky130 + GF180; T2 legs C-32/C-22 stay dead). Run it in sequence, never in parallel: its $0 test (iv) goes first, and money is spent only after DD2 dies. Honest label: a bounded-downside side line, not a path to full-time income. The literally safest path to income is the day job.
FALLBACK.rationale: No candidate is a safe path to meaningful revenue. DD5 is the safest in the bounded-downside, cycle-proof sense. (1) Economics (04_DEEPDIVES/open-memory-ip.md §14.3; models/open-memory-ip.py re-run, exit 0). ARR $41.2k at m18 and $65.7k at m36 in BASE, $54.9k in GLUT and $49.3k in SEVERE, so a 60% DDR5 glut cuts it only ~16%. First revenue m4. Cash-flow positive at m12 with the founder unpaid. Cash low $4.0k at m15 under the cash gate. End cash $88.4k, $60.4k and $45.1k from $40k: conditional on passing, it is the only survivor positive in all three decks. 57% GM. The founder is never paid. A full free release cuts m36 ARR to $34.0k. It depends on one exclusive contract memory engineer by m3. (2) Its failure mode is uncorrelated with DD2's. The buyers are open-PDK tapeout teams (university VLSI labs, SBIR ASIC teams), not SMB-OEM procurement, so an employer refusal tied to the OEM industry need not kill it. (3) Best mission fit of any survivor, with caveats. It uses sense (c), cheaper capital: open PDKs, MPW shuttles and open IP. Its sky130 leg is U.S.-fab silicon at SkyWater. But only 80 of 228 projects a year are U.S.-fab, GF180 is fabbed in Singapore, and characterized sky130 silicon arrives only at m24 after the cash gate. (4) Integrity correction to the record. The phase5 ev_note's '+$5-15k EV' multiplies p by $88k of end cash, which includes the founder's own $40k. The gain if it passes is $48.4k in BASE (+$20.4k GLUT, +$5.1k SEVERE). Run as written, EV is about -$4k to +$1k before time. Run with the $0 test (iv) first, before the $6k contractor spend, it is about +$3k [ESTIMATE]. (5) Why it is not PRIMARY: a ~3x costlier test ($9.1k), 60-71% services revenue, a hard-to-sell asset, and in my estimate a 10-15% pass probability (author 15-25%). (6) Why sequential: DD2's max draw ($33.9k) plus DD5's (~$36k) cannot both fit in $40k, and 15 h/week cannot carry both.
FALLBACK.gate: First, at $0 (send in week 1): test (iv). Get written statements from BOTH UCSC VLSIDA and Open Circuit Design that they do not plan silicon-characterized >=16 KB open macros within 18 months, or a signed exclusivity. Silence by day 14, or any confirmed free release, is FAIL, and DD5 dies at $0. Only if (iv) passes AND DD2 has died: (iii) a contractor-signed extracted-SPICE run on the 16 KB sky130 macro at SS/1.62V/125C and FF/1.98V/-40C, plus a >=1,000-point Monte Carlo, with <=200 h to build the full line. (i) >=3 paid $500 deposits against >=$2k orders, or >=$15k of signed LOIs, from distinct funded teams. (ii) >=2 commercial or SBIR buyers at >=$10k who accept the 'nominal lot measured, corners simulated, refund-capped warranty' licence. If only (ii) fails, pivot to academic-only GF180. After a pass: an exclusive contractor SOW or technical co-founder by m3, else kill; >=1 paying account and >=$4k invoiced by m6; ARR >=$12k by m12; >=5 accounts or ARR >=$20k by m18; any free >=16 KB sky130 release means stopping one-time spend within 30 days.
FALLBACK.spend: $0 now (two emails, ~30 min). If DD2 dies at K0 (by 2026-11-09) or at K1/K6 (2026-12-01), and (iv) has passed: <=$9.1k on the test (hard cap $10k), started within 30 days but never across the academic winter break. If DD2 dies on 2026-12-01, run it 2027-01-11 to 2027-02-10. After a pass: follow the model's cash gate ($2.5k floor), with a total draw of <=~$36k. No T2 money, ever. If DD2 passes, DD5 stays shelved.

MOONSHOT.pick: NONE honestly qualifies. The best available is the C-86 Memory Cost Escalation Index option inside DD2. The red team killed it as designed, and it is admissible only because the record names a concrete, $0-marginal reopen trigger (K3+K4). It would qualify as a MOONSHOT only if K3 and K4 pass on 2026-12-01 and the m9 publication test passes.
MOONSHOT.rationale: No surviving candidate has a venture-scale ceiling. (1) Every T2+ path the study deep-dived was killed. DD5's C-32 gain cell and C-22 ReRAM chiplet have no density or leakage case on sky130 logic rules, C-22's magnet axis is shared with OTP and eFuse, and neither has a buyer (open-memory-ip.md §14.5). DD7's die bank and MCMs fail too: Plan B returns 0.29x of $11.49M, the bank IRR is -26.6% with no bank bought in any scenario, the MCM does not fit its package, and BULL is ~22%/yr gross before dilution (legacy-dram-diebank.md §14.3). (2) The record's own ceiling table says the only credible path above $2M is C-86 becoming the contract reference index, which means displacing TrendForce: '<$0.5M (upside $2-10M)' (03_SCORING.md §6). (3) The red team killed C-86 as designed. RT-VC-DD2-01 (FATAL): the panel reaches 14.2 members by m36, below the 15 needed. There is no precedent for glut upside in 2018-19 or 2023 (RT-VET-DD2-03). The index competes with TrendForce contract prints and open-book pass-through. DD2 §10-§11 keep it only as an option that closes for good at m15. It costs $0 extra because the same 25 DD2 calls carry the K3/K4 asks. (4) It is mission-adjacent (memory pricing), not memory-making. P(K3+K4 pass) ~5%; P(reaching $2M+ ARR) <=1% [ESTIMATE]. (5) The mission-literal alternative, C-36 (U.S.-fab SRAM second source on SkyWater Fab 25), is rejected below: it is alive only because it was never red-teamed. The confidence figure is confidence in the NONE verdict, not in C-86 succeeding.
MOONSHOT.gate: By 2026-12-01, inside DD2's test. K3: >=2 of 10 index prospects sign LOIs naming a live contract or surcharge schedule, each stating why TrendForce prints and open-book pass-through do not serve it. K4: >=10 contribution agreements signed by the legal function, each covering 24 months of line-item memory PO prices from a buyer with >=$250k/yr memory spend, not EMS-turnkey, with no confidentiality conflict; the cell map must also put >=70% of spend in <=4 grade-homogeneous cells, with >=3 cells able to reach 5 contributors. Then at m9 (2027-08-31): the VET publication test (>=3 cells with >=5 independent buyers in >=80% of quarters, and bootstrap noise below one-third of the TrendForce move), plus counsel confirming antitrust safety. Hard close at 2028-02-29 (m15) unless the panel has >=15 members or an executed contract between unaffiliated parties names the index.
MOONSHOT.spend: $0 beyond DD2's test. Spend the $1,000 government-contracts consult and the $5,000 antitrust opinion only after K3 and K4 both pass. Spend <=$6k in total on the index before an executed contract or a published surcharge schedule names it. Outside capital only after paid index licences exist; never on C-36 or any device path without a deep dive and red team first.

honest_framing: For a founder with <$50k, the study's answer to 'make RAM, or something better, in America' is no. The evidence is snippet-grade (nothing in Phase 1 is [VERIFIED]), but it is consistent: the U.S. has no DRAM foundry, no open die supply and no idle display fab; incumbents make DDR5 at ~$1.48/GB and still earn ~82% gross margin at the $8.15/GB glut price; no alternative memory measured comes within 10x of DDR5 on $/GB; and memory carries no Made-in-USA premium (01_LANDSCAPE.md §0). Every device and T2+ path that reached a deep dive was killed, and after two red-team rounds (186 objections, 0 refuted) none of the seven deep dives pays the founder a salary within 36 months in any price scenario. What survives are two memory-adjacent side lines that make nothing: DD2 lifecycle SaaS (~$70k/$150k ARR at m18/m36) and DD5's open-PDK macro service (~$41k/$66k). The scoring that ranked them #3-#5 rewarded cheapness, not venture quality (03_SCORING.md §6). Re-aim the project: drop 'American Memory' as a venture thesis, keep the day job and the $40k, and spend at most ~$3k and ~55 hours testing whether U.S. hardware OEMs will pay cash for memory-lifecycle software; if that fails, stop. If the founder wants the mission more than the income, the only live concepts that literally make memory here (C-36 SRAM on Fab 25, DD5's sky130 leg) need a hardware co-founder and outside capital, and neither has been shown to beat its incumbent.
biggest_unknown: Whether anyone will pay cash, on a recurring basis, for a memory-adjacent product this part-time, non-chip founder can build. The whole study contains no deposit, PO or paid pilot. Every red-team round cut demand inputs that were estimates: DD2 conversion 0.12 to 0.10 and TAM 6,000 to 3,000; DD5 market 298 to 228 projects/yr; DD6 close rate 8% to 6%. For the PRIMARY it reduces to two linked questions. Will the employer sign a carve-out for a product sold into its own industry (K0)? And will >=5 of 25 cold-sourced SMB-OEM procurement contacts put down a refundable $500 at >=$200/month, at least 3 of them in cash, when Octopart is free and SiliconExpert costs ~$250 (K1)?
